about: Plain-language summaries cached by DOI or id. The daily refresh asks GitHub Models once per uncached paper that has an abstract, and stores only a reply that stays inside that abstract. A failed call, or a paper with no abstract, leaves no summary.

items.summary: This is an early study of a drug called VO659 in adults with SCA1, SCA3, or Huntington disease. The registry says the aims are safety, tolerability, and how much of the drug reaches the blood and spinal fluid. It is listed as recruiting, for ages 25 to 60, and the SCA3 criteria ask for mild to moderate ataxia (a SARA score of 3 to 18).

Servier’s page describes S233107 as a drug designed to lower faulty ataxin-3, given into the spinal fluid, in a placebo-controlled first-in-human study. The page lists it as not yet recruiting. People who can take part have a genetic diagnosis of SCA3, are 18 to 65, and can walk without support.

The public CTIS page lists 2025-525111-17-00 as end of trial on 11 September 2026. Denmark, France, Spain, and Portugal are each marked Ended, reason Sponsor Decision, and the recruitment start and end columns are blank. The page still shows an estimated recruitment start of 1 September 2026 and an estimated end of 31 October 2030.

The registry describes a study that plans to look for a dose of transcranial temporal interference stimulation in people with diagnosed SCA3 who already have symptoms. It is listed as not yet recruiting, at one site in China, for ages 18 to 75 with a SARA score of 8 to 30.

The registry describes a study of deep brain stimulation in the deep cerebellar nuclei for people with SCA1 or SCA3 and moderate ataxia. It is listed as not yet recruiting, at two sites in the United States, for ages 18 to 60 with a SARA score of at least 11. The stated purpose is safety and feasibility.

The registry describes a Phase 2 study of umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells for people with SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, or SCA6. It is listed as not yet recruiting, for ages 16 to 60 with a SARA score of 2 to 5, and no sites are listed. The record states an aim to study safety and efficacy.

This recruiting study in France measures eye and balance-reflex findings in people with SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, or SCA27B. The criteria include both people with a SARA score of 4 or higher and people with a score below 4.

In 229 people with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 and 104 healthy adults, thinking, anxiety, fatigue, depression, and sleep declined after ataxia began. Brainstem volume left the healthy pattern 0.7 years before ataxia and a deep brain region (the ventral diencephalon) 0.2 years before, and an inflammation signal in both regions rose and stayed off the healthy pattern through the disease.

Fieldwork and interviews in two regions of Brazil with people who have Berardinelli syndrome, present from birth, or Machado-Joseph disease, which starts in adulthood, and with their families, found that bodily changes were judged in moral terms. People first explained symptoms in everyday terms and later as a genetic illness, stigma tracked bodily change together with expectations about gender, and health activism was one way of coping.

Two compounds, AN2 and GW5074, tagged harmful ataxin-3 with 84 glutamines for the cell's cleanup system and lowered it, but not the normal protein, in cells and in brain cells grown from patient stem cells, where shortened nerve branches partly recovered. In mice, mouth, abdominal, and brain-fluid doses lowered the protein and improved movement, and mouth doses reached the cerebellum at very low (nanomolar) levels with no overt liver, kidney, or support-cell harm over 28 days.

A blood chemical fingerprint, read with a computer classifier, sorted spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 in 202 people, with separation scores (AUC) of 0.952 in the first group and 0.963 in a later group. A shorter panel of 21 chemicals still separated the groups, with scores of 0.901 and 0.932.

In brain tissue from Parkinson's disease and spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, and in related cell models, 19 candidate differences in very short gene pieces called microexons did not hold up after a correction for many tests. A lab check in the cell models detected the chosen pieces and did not confirm a difference between groups, and brain tissue showed many more of these pieces than the cell models.

For 12 months, 56 people with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 took DL-3-n-butylphthalide, 200 mg three times a day, and 60 took a placebo. The treated group did better on the SARA ataxia score (difference -0.86; 95% confidence interval -1.56 to -0.16; P = 0.02) and the SCAFI function score (difference 0.16; 0.01 to 0.31; P = 0.03), and side effects were 23.2% versus 15% (P = 0.26), drug-related side effects were 21.4% versus 10% (P = 0.09), and no serious adverse events occurred.

In brains of Machado-Joseph disease gene carriers, chemical tags on DNA (methylation) changed at only three single sites but across 175 regions, eight shared by two brain areas, and extra tags in the cerebral cortex were concentrated in pathways that build myelin. In blood, no single site reached genome-wide significance, regional changes were stronger before symptoms and did not overlap the brain, 5,241 sites tracked disease duration, and age acceleration, a methylation estimate of faster aging, was not linked to age at onset.

Brain protein profiles from male and female Machado-Joseph disease mice showed shared changes in mitochondria, the cell's energy units, and in energy-making proteins, and nerve cells from those mice had altered mitochondrial shape. Zebrafish neurons making human ataxin-3 with 84 glutamines had changed energy-chain proteins and greater sensitivity to the toxin rotenone, and complex II of that chain was altered in most tests.

Seventy-four people with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 and 45 healthy adults stood on foot-pressure sensors with eyes open and eyes closed. Eyes-closed sway separated patients from healthy adults more accurately than eyes-open sway, some sway measures tracked clinical scores (r greater than 0.4), and a computer model classified disease severity with 87% accuracy.

A 58-year-old woman with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 symptoms for 10 years, already taking troriluzole 200 mg a day, received three monthly intravenous infusions of 70 million donor fat-derived stem cells. Her SARA ataxia score fell from 7.5 to 3.5 by the third infusion, was 4.5 at 3 months and at about 12 months, then rose, while central dizziness and neck dystonia (involuntary tightening) did not improve, and same-day flushes, low fever, queasiness, neck tightness, headache behind the eyes, and a mild pulse and blood pressure rise cleared by the next day.

After screening 34 transport proteins, researchers found higher Importin-8 gene message in Machado-Joseph disease. Lowering Importin-8 reduced ataxin-3 clumps and nerve-cell dysfunction in cells and in living animals, and it lessened ataxia-like movement problems in the animals.

A review of progressive cerebellar ataxias found that the SARA ataxia score tracks gene-specific courses but loses sensitivity at the two ends of the disease. Brain MRI measures and blood neurofilament light chain, a marker of nerve-fiber damage, change before ataxia and predict later decline, repeat length and other genetic modifiers set risk beforehand, and wearable gait and balance sensors detect change earlier than clinical scales and sharply cut the number of people a study needs.

In 129 people with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (44 before ataxia and 85 with ataxia), 51 followed over time, and 78 controls, a brain-scan index of tissue along fluid spaces around vessels was lower once ataxia was present than before ataxia or in controls. A lower index tracked worse symptoms (r = -0.208), smaller brainstem size, and faster worsening over time.

Removing Ficd, which places a chemical tag called AMPylation on the helper protein BiP, improved movement in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 mice and lowered nuclear ataxin-3 in vulnerable brain regions, while littermates that kept Ficd had more tagged BiP in the spinal cord. Removing Ficd also lessened the loss of myelin-building proteins and restored mature myelin-making cells, and Ficd turns on a cholesterol-making pathway that supports myelin.

In brains examined after death, the expanded CAG repeat in Purkinje cells, the main output cells of the cerebellar cortex, grew only minimally in people with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3. The growth was similar to that in cerebellar granule neurons, and the repeat was more stable in Purkinje cells than in medium spiny neurons of the striatum.

In a cell model of spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, 0.3 and 0.5 micromolar omaveloxolone improved survival, reduced cell death, and lowered mutant ataxin-3 more consistently than 0.1 micromolar, and it raised the cell-defense switch Nrf2 and the proteins NQO1, HO-1, and SOD2 without a significant change in reactive oxygen. At 0.3 micromolar, mitochondria partly shifted from round toward elongated forms and gained DNA copies, and in fruit flies with the disease the drug partly improved survival, climbing, eye size, and eye color, with more evident benefits at earlier stages.

Mice with an Atxn3 repeat of 300 glutamines developed worsening sensory and motor nerve problems, peripheral tissue damage, and disrupted RNA splicing that parallel clinical spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, while mice with no ataxin-3 had normal peripheral nerve function. Turning off only the mutant gene in sensory neurons lessened the nerve abnormalities and the splicing problems in the sensory-nerve clusters beside the spinal cord.

Among 84 people with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, grouped by thinking scores against 41 healthy adults, patients with thinking problems differed from patients without them on resting brain scans. Slow signals were higher in frontal-striatal regions and lower in the brain's rest network, a second signal was lower in a side planning area and higher in midline motor areas, cerebellar thinking regions were more locally in sync, the left putamen, insula, and superior frontal gyrus were less connected, and these patterns tracked cognitive scores.

Cinnamon bud extract reduced sheet-like amyloid clumps of ataxin-3 and shifted the protein toward soluble forms that were not fibers, and flavonoids, cinnamaldehyde, and cinnamic acid were the main molecules that bound it. In a roundworm model of spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, the whole extract and a polyphenol-rich fraction improved movement and raised resistance to oxidative and heat stress.

Neck and armpit skin bacteria were sequenced in 30 people with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 and 30 healthy adults of similar age and sex. The neck had a wider, different mix than the armpit (P = 0.001), patients differed from healthy adults at the armpit (P = 0.009) and neck (P = 0.023), 7 bacterial groups tracked with motor severity, disease duration, or CAG repeat length, and site-specific signatures separated patients from healthy adults with a score of 0.84 (95% confidence interval 0.64 to 1.00).

Repeated vein injections of fat-derived stem cells helped SCA3 mice do better on a rotating rod and lowered harmful ataxin-3, a shortened protein with 69 glutamine repeats, inside cerebellar Purkinje cells. The mice also had less loss of the nerve coating myelin and less inflammation in the brain and body, and the blood nerve-injury marker neurofilament light moved opposite to the rotating-rod scores.

A 60-year-old Chinese woman was first treated as having Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease because of reduced feeling in the hands and feet, high-arched feet, and missing reflexes. Cerebellar signs, speech and swallowing trouble, eye-movement problems, and an expanded CAG repeat in the ATXN3 gene later showed she had Machado-Joseph disease, also called SCA3.

Gene maps of the cerebellum showed lower insulin and glucose-control programs, and lower fat and cholesterol programs, in SCA3 mice with 84 glutamine repeats than in control mice with 15. Metabolic models of the same tissue showed less oxygen-based energy use, more nucleotide salvage, one-carbon metabolism, and protein-balance remodeling, along with higher blood insulin and lower Ins2 and Igf1 gene activity.

Compared with 163 healthy people, 117 people with SCA3 had weaker physical brain connections and stronger activity links in deep, movement, and attention networks. Physical links between frontal-parietal and deep networks rose with longer disease and longer CAG repeats, links inside the deep network fell with longer disease, and magnetic brain stimulation weakened two overly strong pathways in 58 patients.

A 62-year-old man with genetically confirmed SCA3 later developed rapidly worsening uneven muscle weakness, muscle wasting, and twitching. Preserved tendon reflexes and widespread loss of muscle nerve supply on an electrical test led to a diagnosis of coexisting sporadic ALS, and a review of published cases found only a few like this.

A lab test measured polyglutamine-expanded ataxin-3 in spinal fluid, blood, and urine from 97 people with SCA3 symptoms and 13 gene carriers without symptoms yet. Asian participants had lower blood levels and higher urine levels than people of other ancestries, and spinal-fluid levels were higher in symptomatic people at the first test and then fell over time.

Cerebellar size scores, based on 2,549 MRI scans from 2,071 healthy people, split 114 people with SCA3 into a group with relative sparing in back lobules VIIB and VIIIA and a group with widespread shrinkage in front motor lobules I through VI who had worse ataxia. The shrinkage group improved more after deep magnetic brain stimulation, both groups improved after repetitive stimulation, the spared group did better with repetitive than deep stimulation, and shrinkage of the right lobule VIIB predicted severity in the shrinkage group.

People with SCA3 showed a split between wiring and activity in the upper outer putamen, a deep movement area, on both sides that did not depend on tissue loss and tracked ICARS ataxia scores, in 117 patients versus 163 healthy people and again in 24 versus 48. That split lined up with mitochondrial complex II, serotonin receptors 5-HT2A and 5-HT4, and genes for synapse control and keeping cells stable.

In 228 Japanese people with SCA3, the PRKN variant V380L was G/G in 86.0%, G/C in 13.2%, and C/C in 2 people (0.9%), similar to 260 people with SCA6 and to East Asian reference groups. Median onset was 42 versus 41 years and the expanded ATXN3 repeat was 71 in both the G/G and G/C groups, and after adjustment the variant was not tied to onset age (change of -0.42 years, p = 0.84), while each extra expanded CAG repeat moved onset earlier by 1.68 years.

A twin prime editor fitted with an La protein domain, plus optimized guide RNAs, raised editing efficiency 1.75 ± 0.21-fold at several sites in human cells, without more unwanted insertions, deletions, or inaccurate edits. The same tool inserted a green fluorescent protein gene of about 2.8 kb and removed the expanded polyglutamine stretch from ATXN3 in a human cell line that models SCA3.

Repeat brain-chemistry scans within two weeks had similar test-retest variation across four sites and two scanner brands, after a small adjustment for the site, in 18 people with SCA2 (mean ataxia score 9 ± 5), 25 with SCA3 (mean 10 ± 6), and 29 controls. Total N-acetylaspartate and glutamate were lower, and myo-inositol and total creatine higher, in the cerebellum and pons than in controls; SCA2 and SCA3 differed on pontine N-acetylaspartate and myo-inositol and on cerebellar N-acetylaspartate, myo-inositol, and glutamate (effect sizes 1.1 to 2.1), and the N-acetylaspartate-to-creatine ratio tracked clinical scores best (correlation at least 0.5), in the cerebellum for SCA2 and the pons for SCA3.

ATXN3 gene carriers with thyroid tests in the normal range had lower TSH, a lower free T3 to free T4 ratio, and higher thyroid secretory capacity than controls, already before ataxia, when that ratio also rose with longer CAG repeats. In people with symptoms, a lower ratio went with faster yearly worsening on the SARA and ICARS ataxia scores, and on follow-up the lower-ratio group had steeper SARA worsening (beta -1.68, 95% confidence interval -2.812 to -0.554, p = 0.007), while the ICARS change was not significant.

In a triple-blind crossover study, 32 people with SCA3 (23 finished) took Astragalus membranaceus or placebo for three months, waited one month, then switched. On the herb, neurofilament light fell from 27.6 ± 10.7 to 25.6 ± 9.8 pg/mL (P = 0.040) and insulin rose from 12.5 ± 15.2 to 21.1 ± 15.5 μIU/mL (P = 0.004), but versus placebo the neurofilament difference was not significant (P = 0.127), neurofilament did not track insulin, and IGF1 and its binding proteins did not change.

Body-wide doses of tiny cell-made packages, coated with a rabies-virus protein to carry miR-370 blockers into the brain, raised the helper protein DNAJB1, reduced mutant ataxin-3 clumps, improved nerve-cell survival, and restored motor coordination in SCA3 mice. Adding miR-25, which targets the ataxin-3 genetic message, lowered harmful ataxin-3 and protected nerve cells more than either treatment alone.

In human microglia, immune cells of the brain, ataxin-3 bound the chloride channel CFTR and sped its breakdown with K63-linked ubiquitin tags, so CFTR did not last as long, and those same tags also sped breakdown of ataxin-3. The disease form with 80 glutamines had a stronger effect than normal ataxin-3 and pushed these immune cells toward an inflammatory state.

Diffusion scans of 42 people with SCA3 and 41 healthy people of similar age and sex showed white-matter damage mainly on the cerebellum-to-thalamus-to-cortex route, with less efficient brain networks and longer paths between regions (each p < 0.001). Efficiency in cerebellar vermis VI fell as CAG repeats (r = -0.62), disease severity (r = -0.58), and motor scores (r = -0.65) rose, each p < 0.001, and the precentral gyrus, cerebellum, hippocampus, and thalamus were also altered (p < 0.05, corrected).

Thirty SCA3 mice, 14 weeks old, received cerebellar magnetic stimulation at 30% of maximum output, 600 pulses a day, five days a week for two weeks, as intermittent bursts, continuous bursts, or sham. Compared with sham, intermittent bursts cut rotating-rod falls, improved gait, lowered ataxin-3 and ubiquitin-tagged clumps, reduced inflammatory signals, and turned on the cell's cleanup system, and most of these gains were also stronger than with continuous bursts; both burst types increased Iba-1 immune cells, and only intermittent bursts raised calming CD206 cells.

Across 30 studies of 432 people with SCA3, including 64 without symptoms yet, the most common findings were a weak eye-steadying reflex on quick head turns (117 of 133), jerking on side gaze (65 of 82), mistargeted fast eye jumps (33 of 49), tiny to-and-fro jumps called square-wave jerks (29 of 45), and weak smooth tracking (14 of 19). Other tests found delayed or slow fast eye jumps (13 of 29 and 16 of 49), rebound jerking (8 of 10), abnormal ear-temperature responses (7 of 9), a weak visually boosted reflex (5 of 6), and weak vestibular responses in neck muscles (19 of 66) and eye muscles (10 of 14).

MRI of 408 people with SCA3 (82 before ataxia) and 293 controls showed one shrinkage pattern that grew stronger over the disease, largest in the pons, cerebellar white matter, and cerebellar peduncles (effect size above 1.5; correlations with severity and duration from -0.65 to -0.40). Cerebellar gray-matter loss was greatest in movement, attention, and emotion areas (effect size about 0.7); outer-brain loss appeared only in the most severe group, striatal loss started early and stayed level, and cerebrum and cerebellum volumes were less linked than in controls.

After adjustment for body mass index, 229 people with SCA3 who already had ataxia had higher LDL cholesterol and lower HDL cholesterol than 316 controls, and a low body mass index had hidden much of that difference. HDL was higher in 37 carriers before ataxia and lower once ataxia was present, lower HDL predicted a higher SARA ataxia score (beta -2.881, P = 0.006), and HDL separated those two stages with an area under the curve of 0.837.

In 324 people with SCA3, higher education went with lower SARA ataxia scores but earlier age at onset, smoking went with earlier onset, and tea drinking went with lower ataxia scores. Body mass index, coffee, alcohol, and the other factors assessed had no association with age at onset or SARA scores.

The authors clarify that a 9-base-pair duplication in ATXN2 was proposed to change the age SCA3 starts only together with an intermediate ATXN2 copy of 29 CAG repeats, and that a claimed protective effect is unsupported because the results were not statistically significant. DNA, RNA, and protein evidence supports the duplication as one genetic modifier of SCA3, and both start sites ATG1 and ATG2 can begin protein production, accounting for an ATXN2 protein of about 140 to 145 kDa.

JOSD2, an enzyme in the Machado-Joseph disease family, removes ubiquitin tags from proteins and adjusts protein balance and cell signals. Reviewed studies link abnormal JOSD2 activity to cancer through changes in metabolism, cancer signals, and treatment resistance, and report both harmful and protective roles in heart and blood-vessel disease and inflammatory bowel disease.

Brain MRI in 92 people with SCA3, 14 before symptoms and 78 with symptoms, and in 98 healthy people showed weaker fluid clearance along blood vessels in both SCA3 groups, and weaker clearance still after symptoms began. Weaker clearance went with worse disability, with longer disease only after 3 years, and with more shrinkage of outer and deep gray matter and more white-matter damage.

Among 182 people with SCA3, 45.6% had double vision, and that group scored higher on ICARS, an ataxia scale. Visual impairment raised the odds of double vision 2.22 times, and double vision tracked with more severe ataxia, by 7.77 points.

Raising the protein Rad23b increased clumps of mutant ataxin-3 and nerve-cell death, while lowering or removing Rad23b reduced both. Rad23b binds mutant ataxin-3, puts a ubiquitin label on it, and delivers it to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, then blocks that shredder so the protein is not broken down, and in SCA3 mice Rad23b sat with the clumps in cerebellar nerve cells.

In 23 people with SCA3, higher NAA/Cr, a nerve-cell marker, and Cho/Cr, a membrane marker, on spectroscopy of the cerebellar cortex, dentate nucleus, and midline vermis went with higher Barthel Index scores of daily independence (correlation 0.66). Regression analyses confirmed that link.

The READISCA study followed 43 healthy people, 55 SCA1 carriers, and 124 SCA3 carriers yearly for 5 years, and ataxia developed in 5 of 22 pre-ataxia SCA1 carriers (22%) and 12 of 38 pre-ataxia SCA3 carriers (32%). Converters were more depressed (score 3.9 versus 2.3), had higher blood neurofilament (17.6 versus 11.1 pg/ml), more cerebellar white-matter loss, and more non-ataxia signs (1.8 versus 0.7), and faster one-year worsening on the SARA ataxia score tracked with disability stage, cerebellar function score, and creatine in cerebellar white matter (model R2 = 0.54).

In two SCA3 mouse models, RNA data, and postmortem brain tissue, CARHSP1, a protein in stress granules, the clumps cells form under stress, was increased in SCA3. Lowering Carhsp1 in the mice reduced mutant protein clumps, improved movement, and lessened nerve damage.

Electrical tests of the sensory path from limb to brain were abnormal in 18 of 20 people with SCA3 (90%) and in 3 of 20 people with SCA10 (15%) at a clinic in southern Brazil. In SCA3 the faults were mostly in the brain and spinal cord part of the path, most people with SCA10 had normal tests, in keeping with ataxia limited to the cerebellum, and abnormal tests showed no link with age, symptoms, scans, or gene measures.

A fat-anchor tag packed the gene editor SpCas9 and its guide RNA into extracellular vesicles, tiny bubbles cells release, and a light-cleavable linker let light free SpCas9 and increased its contact with the ATXN3 gene in cells. Vesicles carrying these tools switched off ATXN3 in stem cells from people with SCA3 and in two SCA3 animal models.

Lung tests in 102 people with SCA3 and 91 healthy people showed lower lung capacity, weaker airflow, poorer gas transfer, and more trapped air, and impaired lung function was present in 71 of 102 patients (69.6%) versus none of the controls. Impairment rose with the SARA ataxia score (odds ratio 1.196, 95% confidence interval 1.038 to 1.376), the diaphragm still worked on ultrasound, a higher neutrophil-to-lymphocyte inflammation count went with lower small-airway flow (correlation -0.272), and 4 SCA3 mice compared with 3 healthy mice had the same lung-function pattern with tissue changes consistent with inflamed airways.

A single nose-spray dose of neuropeptide Y prevented and reversed many behavior problems in male rats in a prolonged-stress model of PTSD, while female rats needed a higher dose or pretreatment with a DPPIV enzyme blocker for the same protection. In limited human studies, nose-spray neuropeptide Y in salt water was well tolerated.

The study identified three extra ATXN3 copies, ATXN3L0, ATXN3L2, and ATXN3L3, made by reinserting the gene into the genome at different points in primate evolution, plus the known copy ATXN3L1. ATXN3 and ATXN3L1 have been preserved through primate evolution and still share about 70% of their amino acids, ATXN3L2 matches ATXN3 at 79% of its DNA letters in a broken reading frame, ATXN3L3 is absent in humans, and the CAG patterns show how human ATXN3 came to carry pure long CAG tracts that cause disease when they expand.

In human cells with normal ataxin-3 (15 glutamines) or disease-length ataxin-3 (77 glutamines), gastrodin was not toxic, cut buildup of the 77-glutamine clumps (p < 0.01), raised the amount of ataxin-3 that stayed dissolved, and raised antioxidant capacity. It selectively lowered the signaling proteins ERK1/2 and p38.

SCA3 cells were less viable and more easily damaged by heat, and in SCA3 mice a large part of one end of the CHIP protein was trapped in clumps inside nerve-cell nuclei while free CHIP fell with age. Cerebellar single-cell gene maps showed a disordered stress response, the three-part form of HSF1 was lower than in healthy cells, and extra CHIP partly restored HSF1 and DNAJB1, a heat-shock helper, repaired the heat-stress response, and improved several disease features.

People with SCA3 had resting brain-wave recordings before and after a 3-week course of magnetic stimulation over the cerebellum or a pretend treatment. Real stimulation raised the strength of beta brain waves and their synchrony between the back of the head and the central and side regions, those features predicted longer-term improvement in ataxia, and people who received the pretend treatment showed none of these changes.

In 100 people (23 with SCA1, 63 with SCA3, median SARA score 5, 42% before ataxia, and 14 controls) scanned over a median of 3 years, lower-brain volumes changed more than the SARA ataxia score, and pons volume changed the most, with effect sizes of 1.09 before ataxia and 1.48 with ataxia. SCA1 progressed faster in the cerebellum and SCA3 in the pons, changes in the cerebellar fiber bridge and in pons chemistry tracked the SARA ataxia score and daily-activity scores (correlation 0.28 to 0.47), a 1-year prevention trial using pons volume would need 73 people per arm to detect a 50% slower decline with 80% power, and early treatment trials using pons volume would need about 6 times fewer people than trials using SARA.

In 32 people with SCA3 and 36 age- and sex-matched controls, blood IGFBP1, IGF2, and free IGF1 were higher, insulin was lower, and the glucose-to-insulin ratio was higher. IGFBP1 rose with the SARA ataxia score and with neurofilament light chain, a nerve-damage protein, and fell as body mass index rose, and people with insulin below 3.65 microunits per milliliter had higher IGFBP1 and neurofilament than people with higher insulin.

Blood tests of 24 metabolic markers in 101 people with SCA3 and 101 healthy controls found significant differences, after a correction for multiple tests, in total and indirect bilirubin, the enzymes AST and LDH, blood sugar (glucose and HbA1c), and the cholesterol markers total cholesterol, HDL, and Apo-A1. Those metabolic differences showed strong links to SCA3 gene measures and to symptoms.

A 10-year-old girl, well below the usual SCA3 onset of 30 to 40 years, came in with an unsteady walk and slurred speech and carried ATXN3 CAG repeats of 20 (normal) and 77 (expanded) plus huntingtin repeats of 19 (normal) and 38 (expanded). Scans showed mild cerebellar shrinkage and bony outgrowths on both shin bones, and the 77-repeat ATXN3 expansion was identified as the main reason her disease started in childhood.

At 13 ataxia centers, 231 people with SCA3 who already had ataxia showed deficits on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment compared with 111 healthy controls, after accounting for age and education, in the total score and in visual planning, attention, language, and abstract thinking. The 61 gene carriers before ataxia showed no comparable deficit, scores fell as ataxia worsened especially in people with less education, and blood and scan measures added no further significant link.

A computer screen of 4,986 SCA3-related proteins and 696 natural-product targets found 239 shared proteins, and a cell-signaling route called MAPK, involving 33 proteins including AKT1, TP53, TNF, EGFR, RELA, and MAPK1, stood out. Of the compounds tested, crocin bound most tightly, at -9.5 kcal/mol with AKT1 and -6.6 kcal/mol with TP53, and further simulations showed those bindings stayed stable and strong.

Eight-month-old Machado-Joseph disease mice given two vein injections of bone-marrow stromal cells, one week apart, walked better on footprint and beam tests and partly recovered blood-vessel structure. Collagen IV on vessel surfaces fell, blood supply in the cerebellum steadied, less Evans blue dye crossed the blood-brain barrier, and the vessel-sealing proteins VE-cadherin, claudin-5, and occludin returned in a pattern that differed by sex.

In 1,439 people in China with SCA3 (1,212 with symptoms and 227 without), the length of a CAG repeat in the TCF4 gene did not by itself change the age symptoms began. Across short (7-13), medium (14-39), and long (40 or more) TCF4 groups, longer TCF4 repeats strengthened the ATXN3 effect from 2.04 to 3.18 years earlier per repeat, and that change was largest when symptoms began at age 25 or younger (an extra adjusted R-squared of 0.048).

Among more than 800 people with SCA3 from different countries, common APOE gene patterns and single APOE copies were not linked with the age symptoms began. In people from Brazil, two copies of APOE epsilon 4, a rare pairing, went with symptoms starting a mean of six years earlier than other APOE patterns.

In test-tube experiments, the chemical DTT, as it oxidized, pushed ataxin-3 into abnormal shapes tied by sulfur bonds in its cysteine-rich Josephin region, and the DTT breakdown product 4,5-dihydroxy-1,2-dithiane directly set off clumping. The chemical TCEP kept ataxin-3's cysteines in their reduced form and slowed clumping, but it also cut the full-length protein, and running the tests at 50 °C removed the dependence on whether the mixture was oxidizing or reducing.

In blood from 38 Azorean carriers of the Machado-Joseph expansion, all 28 people from the Joseph family line made more of the expanded ATXN3 copy, while 8 of 10 people from the Machado line showed the opposite pattern (p < 0.0001). With genetic and clinical data from 76 more Azorean patients, expanded-repeat length alone would put symptom onset later in Joseph carriers, yet both family lines reported similar ages at onset.

Resting brain scans of 14 people with SCA3 and 14 healthy adults, centered on a cerebellar region called Crus I, showed weaker connections between the cerebellum and the rest of the brain in SCA3. The change was most specific to the left side of the frontoparietal network, which links frontal and parietal brain regions.

In SCA3 mice, the stress hormone corticosterone in the blood began rising between 26 and 30 weeks of age, the response to a brief stress stayed intact, and levels returned to normal after a dexamethasone injection at week 35. In a second group, six weeks of unpredictable stress, begun early in the illness, worsened movement only for a time, and that worsening faded as the disease went on.

Sixty-five people with SCA3 at seven centers filmed a home ataxia score twice a day for 14 days, completing 80.2% of the schedule and giving valid scores in 79.2% of 1,459 recordings, with the best completion over 4 days (84.8%). Within a person, scores spanned 3.0 points from lowest to highest (middle half 2.5 to 4.5; 10.7% of the top score) and 1.0 point across the middle half of scores (middle half 0.5 to 1.5; 3.6%), the swings roughly matched patients' own ratings, worse disease and longer CAG repeats went with smaller relative swings, and over a median of 411 days in 11 people the home score detected change more than the clinic score (0.67 versus 0.37).

In 98 eyes from 52 people with SCA3 and 130 eyes from 65 healthy adults, electrical signals from the retina and the visual pathway were much weaker, visual responses were slower, and all measured nerve-fiber sectors around the optic nerve and the macular layers were thinner. These retinal measures tracked with ataxia scores (SARA and ICARS) and a thinking-and-memory score (MoCA), retinal signal size and structure fell as disease lasted longer, slower visual responses went with fewer CAG repeats, and combining retinal function and structure identified SCA3 more accurately.

Spinal cord from people with SCA3 and from SCA3 mice showed early gene-activity changes that worsened over time, in fat handling, inflammation, cell structure, and nucleic-acid processing. Spinal cord from mice missing the Atxn3 gene showed only subtle gene changes with little overlap, so the SCA3 pattern came from harmful extra activity of the mutant protein, and the SCA3 mice also had faulty RNA splicing, especially in genes of the cells that insulate nerves.

MRI of 20 people with spinocerebellar ataxia (1 SCA1, 11 SCA2, 6 SCA3, and 2 SCA7) and 23 matched healthy adults showed larger fluid spaces around deep-brain vessels, more free water, and less orderly nerve fibers, each still significant at a false-discovery cutoff of q = 0.05, while a fluid-flow index called ALPS did not differ. SCA3 had larger white-matter and total vessel-space measures than SCA2 after that cutoff, nerve-fiber order in the SCA2 group fell over time (p < 0.001), and free water and white-matter vessel spaces showed strong group differences.

Among 40 SCA3 mutation carriers (10 before ataxia) and 16 healthy adults, all but one person with ataxia and 60% of those before ataxia had muscle cramps at least weekly. Nerve pain was reported by 20% before ataxia and 16.7% with ataxia, symptoms from the nerves that run automatic body functions averaged 2 before ataxia and 4.7 with ataxia, nerve-damage scores were higher than in healthy adults and tracked with worse self-rated function and higher clinician ataxia scores, and more of those automatic-nerve symptoms tracked with worse daily life and quality of life.

Male Machado-Joseph mice had more cut alpha-II-spectrin, a protein sliced when the calcium-activated enzyme calpain is active, in the blood as early as 12 weeks of age, soon after neurological symptoms began. At 15 weeks the cerebellum showed more cutting of alpha-II-spectrin, beclin-1, and TDP-43, calpain 1 trended higher, and the calpain blocker calpeptin, given from 10 to 12 weeks, improved neurological symptoms and lowered cut alpha-II-spectrin in blood and cerebellum compared with male mice given an inactive solution.

A model trained on gray-matter MRI from 393 healthy people, drawn from 1,418 to match the ages of 223 people with SCA3 and checked in 96 healthy adults, found a larger brain-age gap in SCA3, so the brain looked older than the person's age (p < 0.05). The gap rose with expanded CAG length (r = 0.141, p = 0.037), years of disease (r = 0.201, p = 0.002), and ataxia score (r = 0.304, p < 0.001), fell with later age at onset (r = -0.201, p = 0.003), and 19 of 33 regions showed greater gray-matter loss (p < 0.05).

Models built from MRI of 68 SCA3 mutation carriers and 37 healthy adults found that a simulated mild current at the cerebellum produced generally weaker electric fields in SCA3, especially in the front part of the cerebellum and when the return electrode was on the head. The forehead setup produced the strongest fields and the lower-neck setup the weakest, and skin-to-cerebellum distance, ataxia score, and the occipital angle, a measure of the back of the skull, each independently tracked with field strength.

Marker-free Azure Kinect recordings of 38 people with SCA3 and 42 healthy adults showed a larger side-to-side stability margin in SCA3, along with wider steps and shorter strides. Step width stood out as a sensitive measure for SCA3 screening.

In 129 people with SCA3 (98 with ataxia and 31 before ataxia) and 67 healthy adults, a brain-scan measure of fluid movement along blood vessels fell from healthy adults, to people before ataxia, to people with ataxia. The left side of the brain showed no significant difference between healthy adults and the pre-ataxia group, the ataxia group was lower than the healthy group, and a lower average score went with higher scores on the SARA and ICARS ataxia scales.
